prompt:
Scope
- Backend implementation only: REST resource-level access control for "entries" (CRUD). Do not change front-end code here; however, provide API behaviors and response fields that allow the front end to render other-users' entries read-only.

Preserved constraints and acceptance criteria (must be implemented exactly)
1) Superusers can read (GET list and GET single) entries owned by other users.
2) Superusers attempting to modify (PUT/PATCH) or delete (DELETE) entries owned by other users must receive HTTP 403 with body: {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
3) Superusers may create and modify/delete entries they themselves own (full write access to own entries).
4) Normal (non-superuser) users must not be able to access other users' resources: attempts to GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE another user's entry must return HTTP 404 (no existence leak).
5) Requests for entries that do not exist must return HTTP 404 for all callers.
6) On create (POST), the created entry's owner_id must be the current authenticated user; ignore any owner_id provided in the client payload.
7) Do not alter any other shared API facts or contracts. Keep endpoints, standard HTTP status codes and JSON resource shapes consistent with existing API conventions.

API endpoints and exact behavior to implement
(Assume standard endpoints: GET /entries/, POST /entries/, GET /entries/{id}, PUT /entries/{id}, PATCH /entries/{id}, DELETE /entries/{id}.)

General authentication/authorization primitives
- current_user: object representing the authenticated user for the request. Must include: id (user id) and is_superuser (boolean).
- resource.owner_id: id of the user who owns the resource.

List (GET /entries/)
- If current_user.is_superuser == true:
  - Return all entries (no owner filter).
  - For each entry in the response include an additional boolean field editable indicating whether the current user may edit this entry (editable = resource.owner_id == current_user.id).
- Else (normal user):
  - Return only entries where owner_id == current_user.id.
  - For these entries set editable = true.
- Response: 200 with array of resource objects (each containing owner_id and editable field).

Retrieve single entry (GET /entries/{id})
1) Lookup resource by id.
   - If not found: return 404.
2) If resource.owner_id == current_user.id: return 200 and resource with editable = true.
3) Else if current_user.is_superuser == true: return 200 and resource with editable = false.
4) Else: return 404. (Do not reveal existence to other normal users.)

Create (POST /entries/)
- Ignore owner_id if present in client payload.
- Set new_resource.owner_id = current_user.id.
- Persist resource and return 201 with the created resource (include owner_id and editable = true).
- If creation fails for other reasons, return appropriate error codes per existing API conventions.

Update (PUT/PATCH /entries/{id})
1) Lookup resource by id.
   - If not found: return 404.
2) If resource.owner_id == current_user.id:
   - Apply update. Do NOT allow changing owner_id: either strip owner_id field from payload or override it with resource.owner_id/current_user.id so owner does not change.
   - Return updated resource (200) or other existing API-standard response.
3) Else if current_user.is_superuser == true:
   - Return HTTP 403 with JSON body exactly: {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
   - Do not reveal whether resource exists beyond the 403 for superuser case (403 is explicit requirement here).
4) Else (normal user accessing another user's resource): return 404.

Delete (DELETE /entries/{id})
1) Lookup resource by id.
   - If not found: return 404.
2) If resource.owner_id == current_user.id:
   - Delete the resource. Return 204 No Content (or existing API-standard delete response).
3) Else if current_user.is_superuser == true:
   - Return HTTP 403 with JSON body exactly: {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
4) Else: return 404.

Error payloads and exact text
- For the 403 condition, the body MUST be JSON with the exact key/value: {"detail": "Read-only access"} (matching the requirement).
- For 404, return standard API 404 response body consistent with existing API; do not add explanatory text that reveals resource existence to non-owners.

Implementation notes and recommended code structure (framework-agnostic)
- Centralize permission logic in a helper or policy function. Pseudocode:

  def authorize_and_load_for_read(current_user, resource_id):
      resource = db.get(resource_id)
      if not resource:
          raise HTTP404()
      if resource.owner_id == current_user.id:
          resource.editable = True
          return resource
      if current_user.is_superuser:
          resource.editable = False
          return resource
      raise HTTP404()

  def authorize_and_load_for_write(current_user, resource_id):
      resource = db.get(resource_id)
      if not resource:
          raise HTTP404()
      if resource.owner_id == current_user.id:
          resource.editable = True
          return resource
      if current_user.is_superuser:
          # superuser is allowed to see but not modify another's resource
          raise HTTP403(detail='Read-only access')
      raise HTTP404()

- Use the above helpers in the endpoints. For list endpoints, use an owner-filtered query for non-superusers; for superusers return all and append editable flags per item.
- Always perform the DB fetch (existence check) before returning permission-based 404 vs 403 distinctions per the rules above.

Payload handling requirements
- On POST and PUT/PATCH, strip any owner_id field supplied by client and ensure owner_id is set to current_user.id (for POST) or preserved (for PUT/PATCH on own resource). Never allow owner_id to be changed via client input.

Audit and logging
- Log attempts by superusers to modify another user's resource (403 cases) for audit trail.
- Audit logs should include: acting_user_id, target_resource_id, attempted_method (PUT/DELETE/PATCH), timestamp.

Tests to add (automated)
- Superuser GET other_user_entry => 200, editable=false.
- Superuser PUT other_user_entry => 403 with body {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
- Superuser DELETE other_user_entry => 403 with body {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
- Superuser PUT own_entry => 200 (or existing success code); ensure owner_id unchanged.
- Normal user GET own_entry => 200, editable=true.
- Normal user GET other_entry => 404.
- Normal user PUT/DELETE other_entry => 404.
- Request non-existent id by anyone => 404.
- POST with owner_id set in payload => created resource owner_id == current_user.id.
- List endpoint: superuser returns all entries and each entry contains editable flag; normal user returns only own entries.

Compatibility and roll-out
- Keep response shapes compatible with existing API; adding editable (boolean) is allowed if the front end will use it to render UI read-only state. If adding editable is unacceptable in your API, document that front end must determine editability from owner_id == current_user.id and current_user.is_superuser; otherwise include editable in responses as described.

Edge cases
- PATCH should be treated same as PUT in permission rules.
- If you have soft deletes, ensure permission checks consider currently visible entries only.
- For batch operations, apply same rules per-item; if mixed ownership in a batch update/delete, respond with 403 for superuser attempts on others (per-item handling recommended) and 404 for normal users.

Summary checklist for implementer
- [ ] Implement helpers that enforce the exact rules above.
- [ ] Ensure 403 responses for superuser modifications of others exactly return {"detail": "Read-only access"}.
- [ ] Ensure normal users see 404 for other users' resources and for non-existent resources.
- [ ] On POST, set owner_id = current_user.id regardless of input.
- [ ] Add editable flag to GET responses (optional if API-compatible) or ensure front end can compute editability deterministically from owner_id and current_user.
- [ ] Add unit/integration tests covering every acceptance case listed.

Do not assume or invent other contracts. If any existing API behavior conflicts with these rules, surface that conflict for an explicit decision rather than guessing. Implement exactly the status codes and message for the cases listed above.
